First,


for


some context


:


AI is creating a


[resurgence for “context”](https://www.forrester.com/blogs/the-next-evolution-of-ai-will-rely-on-context-layers/) in the industry lexicon.


Large language models rely


on context to


understand intent, resolve ambiguity, and


generate acc


urate responses.


As consumers and organizations adopt new AI technology, context plays a key role in creating


relevant


customer-brand interactions.


Organizations don’t need to know the most about their consumers or customers, they need to understand their circumstances and surface the right content or service across answer engines, search engines, chatbots, voice assistants, websites, apps, messages, emails, etc.


But u


sing


c


ontext


i


sn’t


new


.


I


n our 2014 report


[The Power Of Customer Context](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-power-of-customer-context/RES114961) , Forrester introduced a novel idea


: Organizations (specifically, marketing functions) should stop obsessing over campaigns, targeting, customer segments, media schedules, and transactions. Instead, they should focus on interactions, customer recognition, customer moments, contextual utility, value exchange, and engagement.


Context


continues to


appear


throughout CX, marketing, and advertising


, from


[contextual ad targeting](https://www.forrester.com/report/forresters-contextual-strategies-hierarchy-of-needs-framework/RES189436) to context sitting at the heart of an


[anatomy of a moment](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-anatomy-of-a-moment/RES177297) to context being a component of


[our formal definition of personalization](https://www.forrester.com/report/a-vision-precedes-purposeful-consumer-personalization-programs/RES186706) :


*t* *he use of a customer’s history, preferences, behaviors, intent, and context to frame, guide, enhance, and anticipate interactions for relevancy and a mutual exchange of value between the customer and organization* .


### **Context** **Can** **Further** **Consumer Personalization** **Tactic** **s** **If Use** **d Strategically**


Despite over a decade of progress


with


organizations trying to


glean more


context and improve personalization


tactics


, consumers remain lukewarm about


the


personaliz


ed interactions they have with brands


. In our new report,


[The State Of US Consumer Personalization, 2026](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-state-of-us-consumer-personalization-2026/RES201116) , only[52% of US online adults](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-consumer-benchmark-survey-2026/SUS196065) say they like when companies personalize interactions, and fewer still are eager to share more personal information to enable those experiences.


Strategically, organizations are out of sorts.


C


ontext


ualization


requires understanding what a


consumer or


customer is trying to accomplish in a specific moment and using that to create useful interactions for them.


But t


oday’s organizations struggle because so many optimize personalization programs to business objectives rather than customer needs.[Eighty percent of US B2C marketing executives](https://www.forrester.com/data-and-insights/surveys/forresters-q2-2026-cmo-pulse-survey/SUS196239) agree that their personalization strategies focus on showing customers what the company wants them to receive rather than what customers want to receive


—


the


total


opposite of contextualization


.


Legacy Forrester research described context as creating a value exchange, where organizations provide useful services and consumers receive utility in return. Today, it’s the same: Consumers just want personalized moments to be


**relevant and valuable** .


While relevancy is straightforward (“Did it apply to me or not?”), value is nebulous. Consumers realize value in myriad ways, such as saving money, gaining convenience, making decisions, completing tasks, achieving goals, or receiving support. Forrester identifies four dimensions of customer value: economic, functional, experiential, and symbolic.


Technologically,


consumer


and organization


use


has


rapidly evolved


.


Today’s[technologies enable organizations](https://www.forrester.com/report/a-technology-overview-of-consumer-personalization/RES179376) to better hone in on relevancy and value (though[customer data privacy regulation](https://www.forrester.com/report/modern-privacy-requirements-change-the-paradigm-for-marketing-and-advertising/RES136528) and[consumers’ increasing awareness of data privacy](https://www.forrester.com/report/forresters-2025-us-consumer-privacy-segmentation/RES119986) work as opposing forces).


P


ersonalization capabilities


now


combine signals that were difficult or impossible to integrate previously, such as historical customer behavior, transaction history, loyalty status, real-time engagement signals, device and channel information, location and environmental context, and AI-generated predictions and recommendations. More advanced AI techniques push organizations to create interactions on the fly and serve bespoke content and services in real time, as needed.


But without a strategy, technology can only help so much with consumer personalization initiatives and using context to its fullest potential.


Despite technology


advancements


,


consumer expectations remain the same: a value exchange of services and utility back then versus relevance and value now


— all hinging on


first


understanding the customer’s context.
